title: Characters at the Cross
transcript: Welcome to this Good Friday meditation. We're going to be thinking of Luke's account of the crucifixion in Luke's Gospel chapter 23, and particularly from verse 26 down to verse 49, and thinking about some of the characters around the cross whom Luke describes. And the first is the passerby in verse 26: As the soldiers led Jesus away, they seized Simon from Cyrene, who was on his way in from the country, and they put the cross on him and made him carry it behind Jesus. So he was just a passerby that day, but it was a day that changed his life. And that could, of course, be true for some of us here this morning or this afternoon, that we're just passing by the church, we're curious about what's going on here. Well, let's follow this passerby as he enters a story that he knew nothing about and indeed had no part in, until that moment when he was grabbed by some passing soldiers. Now, in the Roman Empire, someone who was condemned to death by crucifixion was often compelled to carry the heavy crossbeam that they would get nailed or tied to before they were hoisted up on it until they died of dehydration and asphyxia. So Jesus, well, he would have been exhausted and bleeding heavily from the flogging and the crown of thorns on his head. So at some point he collapses under the weight of that crossbeam and he can't carry on. And so into this story of the crucifixion, this pivotal moment in all history, steps a passerby. The soldiers just grab a man who was not even local, but who seems to have got caught up in the crowd. Luke tells us that he was on his way in from the country. He was probably a pilgrim planning to be in Jerusalem for the Passover, probably there with his family. And so they make him carry that heavy crossbar, walking behind Jesus, who somehow manages to stumble on towards Golgotha. Now surely we might think this is a completely incidental detail. I mean, this is just an unknown passerby who, he'll just come and go from the story after being compelled to do a favor for one of those three wretched on that bloody street out of the city? But no, 3 of the Gospels—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—all record this detail, and they tell us the name of this passerby and where he had come from. He was Simon from Cyrene, which is in North Africa, more or less where Libya is today. Now, when people are named in the Gospels, It's because they were known, known to the followers of Jesus who preserved these memories and eventually wrote them down in what we call the Gospels. And Mark was the earliest of those who wrote down the good news about Jesus and especially his account of the crucifixion and resurrection. And there's a strong tradition, which is almost certainly true, that Mark wrote his Gospel in Rome on the basis of the eyewitness memories of Peter. One of the closest of all Jesus' disciples. And it's Mark who gives us the most interesting details about this passerby who carried Jesus' cross. Mark says, "A certain man from Cyrene, Simon, the father of Alexander and Rufus, was passing by on his way in from the country, and they forced him to carry the cross." But How would Mark, or anybody, know the name of this passerby, and not only know where he had come from, but also know the names of his two sons, Alexander and Rufus? And the answer can only be, really, that sometime after this terrible day, Simon and his family joined those disciples of Jesus such that they came to know his identity. Simon, who followed Jesus to his crucifixion, became a follower of Jesus after his resurrection. And as I said, Mark most probably wrote his Gospel in Rome among the community of believers in that city. And as we know, the Apostle Paul wrote his longest and his most famous letter to that community. We call it his letter to the Romans. And at the end of that letter, Paul greets a large number of named believers, men and women, who were known personally to himself and some who had served with him in spreading the gospel and had suffered for it. And among them Paul names, quote, "Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who has been a mother to me too." That's in Romans 16:13. Could this be the same Rufus who was known and named by Mark? The same Rufus who was the son of Simon from Cyrene and Simon's wife? Well, we can't be sure. Of course we can't. But I like to think so. And at any rate, it is certain from the way that Mark, along with all the Gospels apart from John, specifically name Simon, that he was known to the other disciples and indeed became one of them. Simon became a disciple of Jesus as a result of what happened to him and what he witnessed on that first Good Friday. Now, earlier in his Gospel, Luke records Jesus as saying this. Jesus said, "Whoever wants to come after me"—that is, to be my disciple, as it's translated in the NIV—"whoever wants to come after me must deny themselves and take up their cross daily and follow me." Literally, that is, whoever is willing to come behind me And that's exactly what Luke says the soldiers forced Simon to do in verse 26—to follow Jesus by walking behind him carrying the cross. In other words, Simon was the first person to literally do what Jesus said it would mean to be his disciple. Okay, he was forced to do it at first, but somehow Whether on that day itself, as he carried the cross on which he watched Jesus die, or at some point later, Simon turned that literal experience into his spiritual life's journey from then on, which was one of following Jesus as a disciple. Now for us, of course, it's neither literal or forced, but still Simon does show us what it means to be a Christian. Because as Jesus said, it starts with denying ourselves. Not because some Roman soldiers compel us to, but because we can't say yes to Jesus without first saying no to the self-centered, self-promoting ways of our self-absorbed lives. Jesus calls us to deny ourselves. And then also it means to follow in the footsteps of Jesus to the cross and to realize that he died there for me, bearing the weight of my sin and my selfishness, and indeed the weight of the sin of the world, no less. And then, to be a disciple means to walk on from the cross, as Simon must have done, to live a life that's shaped by the love and the self-sacrifice that took Jesus to the cross. That is, to live for Christ. And in Christ. So today then, Simon calls us to walk with Jesus, not just for these 3 hours of our service, but as we go out into the rest of our lives and in every aspect of our lives, to be followers of Jesus crucified and risen. Our second meditation is of the woman In verses 27 to 31, where we read: A large number of people followed Jesus, including women, who mourned and wailed for him. Jesus turned and said to them, 'Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me; weep for yourselves and for your children. For the time will come when you will say, "Blessed are the childless women, the wombs that never bore, and the breasts that never nursed. Then, quote, they will say to the mountains, 'Fall on us,' and to the hills, 'Cover us.' For if people do these things when the tree is green, what will happen when it is dry? Including women, says Luke, as he describes the crowd that followed Jesus and the other two convicted criminals out of the city of Jerusalem to the place of crucifixion. And including women is what Luke does in a number of places in a way that seems to have been very significant to him. For example, back in Luke 8:1-3, Luke makes this observation. He says, Jesus traveled about from one town and village to another, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom of God. And the 12 were with him, and also some women. Who had been cured of evil spirits and diseases. Mary called Magdalene, from whom 7 demons had come out. Joanna, the wife of Cusa, the manager of Herod's household. Susanna, and many others. These women were helping to support them, that is, Jesus and his disciples, out of their own means. So no doubt it's these women who were still there right to the bitter end. And indeed, Luke mentions them again after the bitter end, because after Jesus' body had been taken down from the cross, after he had died, we read at the end of this same chapter, Luke chapter 23, quotes, that the woman who had come with Jesus from Galilee followed Joseph of Arimathea and saw the tomb and how Jesus' body was laid in it. And then they went home and prepared spices and perfumes. Which of course was to anoint the corpse. But they rested on the Sabbath in obedience to the commandment. And then in Luke's next glorious chapter, Luke chapter 24, it's these women again who are the first amazed witnesses of the empty tomb, the first human beings to hear those words of the angels, "He is risen," and the first evangelists to bring the good news to the rest of his disciples. But that's in Luke chapter 24. We're still in chapter 23. And at this moment, on this Friday, these are broken women. They're watching all their faith in Jesus, all the hopes that they had of his kingdom coming, it's all being dashed to the ground. As he collapsed in his own blood under the weight of the cross. So Luke says, "They mourned and wailed for him." Well, of course they did. They were distraught with grief. And we don't need much imagination to picture the sight and sound of their crying when we see it so often these days on our TV screens, don't we? As bereaved mothers and wives cry out in agony over children and husbands who have been slaughtered in yet another missile attack. Somewhere in the world. So they weep and they mourn, but Jesus stops and he turns to them with words that were hardly comforting, were they? He says, "Don't weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children." And what he meant is that, well, much worse than this was going to happen in this city of Jerusalem. Now, this is now actually the fourth time in the Gospels that Jesus has predicted the coming siege and destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans, which is an event that did indeed take place in 70 AD, which is about less than 40 years after Jesus' death. And what Jesus is saying is, look, when that happens, it will be so terrible that women who are now the objects of pity because they've got no children will actually be considered the lucky ones. Because they'll have no mouths to feed like those who are mothers, and they won't have to watch their children suffer and die of starvation during that siege that was going to come. And then Jesus quotes from a text from the prophet Hosea when the city of Samaria in the northern kingdom of Israel had been destroyed by their enemies, which at that time was the Assyrians. This was actually about 700 years earlier. And at that time, people in that siege of Sumeria would be so distressed that, says Hosea in Hosea 10:8, "They will say to the mountains, 'Fall on us,' and to the hills, 'Cover us.'" So Jesus takes that text from the distant past and applies it to the not-so-distant future. That's going to happen again, is what he means. It'll be just like that for Jerusalem. People will wish that they could be dead and buried rather than having to suffer all the horrors of the siege. And then, then Jesus quotes a proverb in verse 31 about green wood and dry wood, a proverb which probably means something like, 'If you think this is bad, far worse is to come.' But what could be worse than the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD? I mean, there are descriptions of that event in contemporary writings, and the descriptions we have of it, of the brutality of that siege, are horrifying in the extreme. So what could be worse? Well, the next time that that verse, the verse that Jesus quoted from Hosea chapter 10, the next time that's found is in Revelation chapter 6, verse 16. And there it's describing the last judgment. Then it's talking about the cry of those who reject God and reject God's Savior, as these people were doing on this very day, and remain unrepentant and unforgiven. Then, says the Bible, then, says Revelation, they will face the wrath of God on that great and final day of judgment, a day that will be far worse than the fall of Samaria in 721 BC or the fall of Jerusalem in 70 AD. Because in that day, says Revelation, they will want to be buried rather than face the living God. But they will find no escape, because in that day evil and evildoers will not go unpunished forever in God's universe. So you see, these words of Jesus to those women were, on the one hand, a very serious warning, and yet They're also a veiled comfort, since they, those women, they were still with Jesus, and they would stay with him right through to his resurrection, when their faith and their love for him would be vindicated and they would be safe. And so his warning to them, which still stands for us, is that even though it was unspeakably horrible for them to watch his suffering, Or indeed, for us to remember it on this Good Friday, there is worse to come—not just the destruction of Jerusalem in the near future, but the final day of judgment in the ultimate future. And on that day, only two possible destinies await us: either, as Hosea and Jesus and Revelation portrayed, we will find no shelter from the judgment of God when we stand before Him on that last day. Or we will have found shelter under the cross, the cross on which Christ bore the judgment of God for us. And that shelter, that eternal safety, is ours when we follow Jesus to the cross, as these women did, as we confess that he died there bearing our sins in our place, and reach out to him in repentance and faith. Our third meditation is of the soldiers. In Luke 23:32-34, where we read: Two other men, both criminals, were also led out with him to be executed. And when they came to the place called the Skull, they crucified him there along with the criminals, one on his right and the other on his left. Jesus said, 'Father, forgive them, For they do not know what they are doing.' And they, that is the soldiers, they divided up his clothes by casting lots. So when they came to the place called the Skull, they crucified him there. Now Luke was writing during the Roman Empire, and people knew what crucifixion was. They would have seen it happen many times because it was an intentionally very public thing. So people reading Luke's Gospel at that time, they didn't need the details of the nails and the blood and excrement and flies and agony and thirst. No, no, Luke doesn't dwell on the appalling, humiliating cruelty of it all. He just reports it. They crucified him there. And then even as they were crucifying him, Jesus prays, 'Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they're doing.' And we're astonished by this, aren't we? I mean, rightly astonished, because, well, how could anybody say this? How could Jesus possibly utter such a prayer, for the people were inflicting such extreme agony on him at that moment? But actually, it's all the more astonishing because it's quite unprecedented. You see, there's nothing at all like this even in the Scriptures of the Old Testament that Jesus knew so well. I mean, if we go back to Old Testament times, what were you supposed to do, or rather, what were you allowed to do when people falsely accused you or violently attacked you or even wanted to kill you, just as was now happening to Jesus? Well, first of all, what you were not allowed to do was to take it upon yourself to avenge the wrong by yourself. Violent retaliation was prohibited. "Do not take revenge," says the law of the Old Testament. Leave it to God. He is the judge and he will take appropriate action to avenge you if necessary. So you could not take revenge yourself, but you certainly could ask God to do it for you. And sometimes they did. I mean, that's what we find in some of the Psalms, don't we? People who are being terribly wronged cry out to God and ask God to act on their behalf, to punish the wrongdoers, to vindicate the innocent. In many ways, they were simply asking God, in a sense, to hurry up and for God to do what He had said He would do. Which is to punish the wicked for their wickedness. So Jesus knew those Psalms. He knew them all. He would have sung them in the synagogue every Sabbath. So Jesus could have prayed words like these from Psalm 28:4 about these soldiers: Repay them for their deeds and for their evil work. Repay them for what their hands have done. Bring back on them what they deserve. I mean, it would have been perfectly understandable if Jesus had prayed that, wouldn't it? And it was from the Scriptures. Or Jesus could have prayed like Jeremiah. When he, Jeremiah, was suffering persecution and physical beatings and death threats, he prayed, "Lord, bring on them the day of disaster. Destroy them with double destruction." That's Jeremiah 17:18. And Jesus would have known about the martyrs during the Maccabean Revolt nearly 200 years before His day. They had fought in a great rebellion and some of them, when they were caught and then were tortured to death, they died calling down God's vengeance on their murderers. But Jesus, who knew the Scriptures and knew His history, He transcends all that. Jesus prays for his executioners, "Father, forgive them." And in doing so, of course, Jesus set a whole new standard, a whole new paradigm for how his followers are to respond to those who hate and kill them. Indeed, Jesus here is modeling exactly what he himself had taught his disciples. Do you remember in the Sermon on the Mount he said, "Love your enemies." 'Bless those who curse you, pray for those who persecute you.' Except that Jesus here is praying for those who are not just cursing and persecuting him, but nailing his hands and his feet to two planks of wood. And then we remember Stephen. Stephen, who was the first Christian martyr in the book of Acts, he followed the example of his master. Luke tells us that as they were stoning Stephen to death, he prayed, "Lord, do not hold their sin against them." That's to say, he was praying for God to forgive his killers, just like Jesus. And only Jesus can enable somebody to think and to speak and to pray like that, whether then or now. But Coming back to our text, Jesus prays, "Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they're doing." Well, no indeed, they didn't. For what they were doing at that moment was nothing less than accomplishing at a human level the deeper will and purpose of God. You see, we know that the cross was a monstrous evil, a complete miscarriage of justice. It was a terrible, bad, evil thing. But it was no accident, because behind the crucifixion stood the sovereign plan of God from all eternity. God's plan that God himself would bear the sin of the world in the person of God the Son. And that's how Peter puts it on the day of Pentecost when he was preaching to those who in fact would have been among those who had called for Jesus to be crucified. And Peter says, "This man, Jesus, was handed over to you by God's deliberate plan and foreknowledge. And you, with the help of wicked men, put him to death by nailing him to the cross." God's deliberate plan and foreknowledge, wicked men nailing him to the cross. And you see, that's the mystery. The mystery of how the worst of all evil, could be the means by which God accomplished the greatest of all good—the redemption of the world. So you see, in putting Jesus to death on the cross, those soldiers were actually carrying out the means by which Jesus' prayer could be answered. Jesus prayed that they should be forgiven, and Jesus died so that they could be forgiven. And then in stark contrast to the divine majesty of that prayer, "Father, forgive them," Luke adds a trivial detail. At least it looks pretty trivial, doesn't it? "They divided up his clothes by casting lots." You see, these soldiers, well, they would have done this many times before. This was just a morning's work for these guys. Banging nails into a few terrorists and hanging them up to die. But the trouble was, you see, that it could take a crucified man a long time to die, and so a spot of gambling would relieve the boredom. So they gathered up Jesus' clothing, and the lucky soldier who won the toss or the roll of the dice, well, could make a few shekels out of those bits and pieces in the marketplace that evening. But this, this is far from trivial. You see, Luke wants us to hear in his words, "They divided up his clothes among them by lot." Luke wants us to hear an echo of Psalm 22. Here's what you read there in verses 16 to 18: All my bones are on display; people stare and gloat over me. They divide my clothes among them, and they cast lots for my garments. That's Psalm 22. Now Psalm 22 is the one which opens with the words, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" And we know from Mark's Gospel that Jesus cried out those very words during his crucifixion. But this Psalm, Psalm 22, is also the one that ends with the words, "It is accomplished. God has done it." And John tells us that Jesus cried those words at the climax of his suffering before he breathed his last. "It is finished, it's accomplished," he said. So this psalm, Psalm 22, from its first verse to its last verse, was already filling the consciousness of Jesus. It was in his heart, it was in his mind, it was on his lips. So here's the psalm, you see, which expresses terrible suffering, the suffering that Jesus was enduring at that moment. But it also expresses confidence in God, because the very next verse of that psalm says, "But you, O Lord, be not far off; deliver my life from death." And indeed, God did exactly that. Not by delivering Jesus from dying, but by taking him through death by the power of his resurrection into the glorious victory that will reach to the ends of the earth, which is what the psalm also says. So you see, Psalm 22 speaks of both appalling suffering but also incredible triumph. So although Jesus died in agony, he did not die in despair. He died trusting in his Father and in the future triumph of the gospel to the very ends of the earth. So there we have it in that one single verse about the soldiers, verse 34 of Luke chapter 23. That one verse Luke offers us both the assurance of the words of Jesus himself that we can be forgiven through his death, and also offers us the assurance of the psalm that Jesus quotes, that death was not the end for him, and so death need not be the end for all of us who put our trust in him. Our fourth meditation is concerning the mockers, and that's in verses 35 to 39. The people stood watching, and the rulers even sneered at him. They said, 'He saved others; let him save himself if he's God's Messiah, the Chosen One.' The soldiers also came up and mocked him. They offered him wine vinegar, and they said, "If you are the king of the Jews, save yourself!" There was a written notice above him which read, "This is the king of the Jews." And one of the criminals who hung there hurled insults at him, "Aren't you the Messiah? Save yourself and us!" Crucifixion was not only brutal, it was nakedly humiliating and shaming by intention. I mean, that was its purpose. It was intended to be a gruesome deterrent. And it seems that Jesus was being mocked and jeered on all sides. Luke records 3 taunts. And in them, I think we can hear an echo of those first 3 temptations by the devil in the wilderness at the very start of Jesus' ministry. Do you remember that back then the devil kept on saying, "If you are the Son of God, if you are the Son of God, you don't need to suffer and die. Just do what I suggest and you'll be fine." That was the devil's temptation back then. And even now, at the very last, when he's actually nailed to the cross, those temptations return ferociously because people are jeering at him. "If he's God's Messiah, if you are the King of the Jews, just come down and prove it." Now those three taunts come from three groups of people, all of whom actually hated each other. But they're now united in hating Jesus. They all say much the same thing, really, but in each case there's a sharp irony between what they think they're saying and the actual truth of the situation. So first of all, there's the religious rulers there in verse 35. They sneer at him: "He saved others, let him save himself." Himself if He is the Christ, the chosen one of God. You see, their mockery was a rejection of the claims of Jesus. What, He thinks He's the Messiah, does He? He thinks He's God's chosen one, does He? He thinks He's the Savior? And they laugh at the whole idea. I mean, look where He is now, spiked up on a Roman cross, powerless to save himself, let alone save anybody else. But of course, that is exactly what Jesus was and is. That is, God's chosen Messiah and Savior. And so the tragic irony is that these religious rulers, they both state the truth about Jesus and reject the truth about Jesus in the same breath. And how dangerous, how scary is that? And then secondly, there's the Roman soldiers in verses 36 to 38. And their mockery is a rejection of the charge that had been made against Jesus, that is, that he was supposed to be the King of the Jews. I mean, that's what was nailed up on the cross just above his head, on possibly a piece of parchment or maybe a piece of wood. It said there, "This is Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews." "But that's ridiculous," they laugh. "King of the Jews? I mean, look at you now. Some king you are, stuck up there with thorns for a crown and a cross for a throne." But again, you see, the irony is that what they said and what had been written above the head of Jesus was actually stating the simple truth. He was and he is the King, the Messianic King, not just King of the Jews, King of the universe, in fact. And then thirdly, There's the criminal in verse 39, the other criminal, or perhaps a terrorist, because the word that's used to describe these men is they're almost certainly political criminals, that is, rebels, zealots, fighters against Rome. We might call them terrorists in our kind of way of speaking today. And one of them, one of them hurls insults at Jesus, and his mockery was an attack on the failure of Jesus. It's as if he's accusing him of saying, "Look, you should have joined us if you'd been any kind of real Messiah. I mean, look, you had your chance, didn't you, a week ago when all the crowds cheered you into Jerusalem? But then you blew it, didn't you? You sneaked off somewhere instead. Okay then, now you've got one last chance to prove that you really are the Messiah. Save yourself." Save us too, while you're about it. Let's all leap down off the crosses and fight the Romans. Ha ha ha! As if! He's mocking Jesus for failing to do what he thought a real Messiah should do. But of course, the irony is that the only way Jesus could be the real Messiah, the that God had planned was by not saving himself, but by going through that suffering and death as Jesus had always said to his followers that he would have to do. So, 3 taunts, 3 temptations, 3 surprising ironies. But there's one more thing here. All 3 of these voices were taunting Jesus to save himself. But that third one, the one that came from the unrepentant criminal, was, "Save yourself and us! Save yourself and us!" But of course, that was precisely what Jesus could not do. He could not both save himself and save us. One or the other, but not both. Now, let's be quite clear at this point. Jesus could have saved himself. There's no doubt about that. Jesus knew it. In fact, at the time of his arrest, you remember Jesus had said to his disciples in Matthew's Gospel, "Do you think that I cannot call on my Father and he will at once put at my disposal more than 12 legions of angels?" I mean, Jesus knows that he's only got to click his fingers and there'll be a dozen battalions of heaven's host there to rescue him. So even at this moment on the cross, as Jesus heard those taunts to save himself, he knew that he could have done so at any moment. Could have saved himself from the agony. He could have saved himself from the mockery and the torture. He could have saved himself from death. Jesus could have saved himself. But if he had, then he could not have saved us. For it was by bearing our sins in his own body on the tree, as Peter puts it, that we are saved. For after all, wasn't that the very reason that Jesus said he had come? He said, "I have come to seek and to save the lost." But if Jesus was going to save the lost, then he could not save himself. And so Jesus chose not to save himself. Jesus chose to die. He chose to stay on the cross for my sake and for your sake, for the sake of those who were crucifying him, and for the sake of those he was being crucified among. As Isaiah puts it, he was pierced for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities, and the punishment that brought us peace was upon him, and by his wounds we are healed. So you see, by not doing what those two criminals wanted, he was able to do what they needed, which is to provide for them through his death a way by which they could be saved, which one of them took, as we shall see later. Our fifth meditation concerns the sun and the curtain in verses 44 and 45, where we read: It was now about noon, and darkness came over the whole land until 3 in the afternoon, for the sun stopped shining. And the curtain of the temple was torn in two, Jesus called out with a loud voice, "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit." And when he had said this, he breathed his last. So human beings were not the only characters at the cross. Luke mentions two others who play a very significant part: the sun in the sky and the curtain in the temple. For 3 long hours, Jesus had endured the agony, the growing heat of the sun, the relentless jeering of the crowds, until at midday God says, "Enough! Enough of this mockery!" And he switches off the light, and the whole scene is drenched in a mysterious miraculous darkness. And I imagine that the noise of the mockery and jeering probably died away and was replaced with a profound fear as God took his Son under the COVID of darkness. Luke simply says the sun stopped shining. Well, as well it might. For its Creator was dying. After all, who was this man on that central cross? Well, let the apostles Paul and John remind us. Paul tells us that for him, in him, in Christ, all things were created, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible. All things have been created through him and for him. And John tells us, "Through him all things were made; without him nothing was made that has been made. In him was life, and that life was the light of men." But now, that light, the true light that gives light to everyone, as John says, Jesus himself, the uncreated source of the light of the sun itself, was dying. And creation responds. The earth quakes. The sun stops shining. For their Creator himself was bearing the cost of reconciling the whole creation to himself through Christ's blood shed on the cross. And creation itself goes into mourning, as it were. And puts on the blackness of cosmic grief. The sun stopped shining. But there was more to that darkness for those who knew their scriptures. You see, those 3 hours of darkness, they're reminiscent of the 3 days of darkness that had been the 9th plague on Egypt. Do you remember how God had brought a fearful darkness upon the land of Egypt, a darkness that spoke of his divine anger and judgment against those who were hardening their hearts against Him and oppressing His people? And so, just as darkness then spoke of God's judgment on the Egyptians for what they were doing to God's people Israel, so darkness now at the cross speaks of God's judgment on Israel for what they were doing to God's Messiah, Jesus. The prophet Amos also speaks of the darkness of God's judgment as a feature of the terrible "day of the Lord," as he calls it. "In that day," says Amos, "in that day declares the Sovereign Lord, I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight." That's Amos 8:9-10. Darkness at noon, then, was an unmistakable sign of the judgment of God. But on whom was this judgment falling? Not just on the Romans, or the religious leaders, or the crowds standing around the cross. Mark tells us that out of this darkness, and after it had rained for 3 hours, came this terrible cry: 'Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani,' which means, 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' And in that cry we realize that this engulfing darkness of God's judgment was being borne by Jesus Himself. For this was the darkness of separation from His Father. And here, at this point, here's where we move with trembling, with awe, with mystery into the deepest depths of the cross. Because it's beyond the physical pain of the flogging and the crucifixion, and beyond the humiliation of those 3 long hours of public mockery, that Jesus now enters the deepest darkness. Of an infinitely greater suffering, and that is the agony of separation from his Father God. The Son of God, who had never known anything in all eternity but the sunshine, the love, the joy of his Father's presence, now sinks into the abyss of his Father's absence. Cut off, severed from his Father. And from that darkness, he can only cry, "Why?" Why indeed? There's only one thing that can separate a human being from God, and that's sin. As Isaiah puts it, "Your iniquities have separated you from your God. Your sins have hidden his face from you so that he will not hear."
